lesson.title: Instance Attributes: Each Object's Own Variables
lesson.summary: An instance attribute is a piece of data stored on one specific object, created with an assignment like self.name = name, so every object keeps its own independent values even though they were built from the same class.
lesson.body:
When __init__ runs the line self.name = name, that is ordinary variable assignment, the same operation you use everywhere else in Python, just aimed at a slightly different target. Instead of creating a local variable that disappears when the function ends, self.name = name stores the value inside the specific object that self refers to, in a private storage space that belongs to that object alone. A value stored this way is called an instance attribute, because it is attached to one particular instance rather than shared by the class as a whole.

```python
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

rex = Dog("Rex")
fido = Dog("Fido")

rex.name = "Rex the Second"
print(rex.name)
print(fido.name)
print(rex.__dict__)
print(fido.__dict__)
```

```
Rex the Second
Fido
{'name': 'Rex the Second'}
{'name': 'Fido'}
```

Reassigning rex.name after the object already exists changes only rex, leaving fido.name untouched, because each object keeps its own separate storage for its attributes. That storage is not hidden magic either: every object has a built-in __dict__ attribute, an ordinary dictionary mapping attribute names to their values, and printing it shows exactly what is stored on that object. rex.__dict__ and fido.__dict__ are two different dictionaries with two different values for the key "name", which is the concrete reason changing one object never affects another.

Although instance attributes are usually set inside __init__ so that every object starts out consistent, self.attribute = value works anywhere a method has access to self, and as rex.name = "Rex the Second" shows, you can even assign to an instance attribute from outside the class entirely, using dot notation on the object directly. Either way, the underlying mechanism is the same variable assignment you have used all along, just scoped to one object's own private dictionary instead of a function or the module as a whole.
